name: Strengths-based therapy
heroTitle: Take the difficulty seriously. Notice what can support you.
summary: A strengths-based perspective considers abilities, relationships, and resources alongside needs. Explore how it differs from positive thinking, minimizing hardship, or making everything your responsibility.
panelTitle: A strength can be ordinary, shared, or still developing.
panelParagraphs: Knowing when to ask for help, identifying a limit, or returning to a routine can matter. Strength is not a demand to manage everything alone.

model.title: Resources and difficulties belong in the same picture.
paragraphs: A strengths-based approach looks beyond deficits to consider a person's abilities, experience, relationships, and available support. It is a broad way of working across services rather than one standardized psychotherapy protocol. The question is what can support change while taking the current difficulty seriously.

The word strengths should not be used to turn suffering into a compulsory success story. A person may be resourceful and exhausted, capable and unsupported, or hopeful and grieving. Both sides can remain true. The work considers not only personal capacities but whether the surrounding conditions allow them to be used.

Resources can include supportive people, practical assistance, meaningful routines, cultural knowledge, or community connections. A plan that identifies only internal strengths may overlook an important shortage of time, money, safety, or access. Recognizing that shortage is information, not a failure of positivity.

panel.title: A capacity is not an unlimited supply.
paragraphs: Being good at caring for others does not remove the need for rest or shared responsibility. Sometimes using a strength differently means protecting a boundary.

example.title: The person everyone relies on is running out of room.
example.intro: A fictional example about caregiving responsibilities, not a plan for a particular family's care.

items.title: The difficulty
paragraphs: Milan manages appointments and errands for a relative while working full time. They describe themselves as disorganized because tasks keep slipping.

items.title: The fuller picture
paragraphs: The conversation reveals careful planning, persistence, and a few people who could share tasks. The workload, however, exceeds what one person can reliably carry.

items.title: A different direction
paragraphs: The work considers how to use those planning skills to coordinate shared support instead of demanding that Milan become even more efficient at doing everything alone.

reveal.title: What makes this strengths-based rather than simply encouraging?
paragraphs: The resources change the practical picture. A support person needs a specific request, a manageable role, and a real agreement. Milan's ability to organize may help, but the actual availability of help matters as much as willingness to ask.

The result is not a guarantee that enough support will appear. If it does not, the plan may need outside resources or a reconsideration of responsibilities. Naming strengths should make a plan more realistic, not hide its limits.

toolsTitle: Look for evidence, access, and a useful purpose.
toolsIntro: These are areas to explore collaboratively, not qualities you have to prove before receiving support.

tools.title: Abilities already in use
tools.teaser: Notice a concrete action rather than a flattering label.
paragraphs: Instead of calling someone resilient, a clinician might explore what they did during a difficult period, what it cost, and what helped. Specific details show how an ability works and when it is available.
The same strategy may help in one setting and become exhausting in another.

tools.title: Relationships and resources
tools.teaser: Include what other people and systems can contribute.
paragraphs: Support is not solely an individual skill. The work can consider who is available, what they can actually offer, and which services or community resources might matter.
An unavailable resource should not be described as a solution simply because it would be helpful in theory.

tools.title: Exceptions and transferable learning
tools.teaser: Learn from a more manageable moment without demanding its repetition.
paragraphs: A less difficult day may reveal useful conditions or responses. The clinician can explore which ingredients might transfer to another situation and which depended on circumstances outside your control.
An exception does not prove you could solve the problem every time if you tried harder.

tools.title: Goals with room for limits
tools.teaser: Use resources to support a life you recognize as worthwhile.
paragraphs: A goal might involve setting a boundary, sharing a responsibility, or returning to something meaningful. It should be specific enough to review without becoming another demand for perfect functioning.
Progress can include recognizing a limit sooner rather than increasing how much you tolerate.

processTitle: A strengths-based plan should become more concrete, not more cheerful.

process.title: Understand the need
paragraphs: Clarify what is difficult and why support is being sought. Assessment and attention to risk are not displaced by a focus on resources.

process.title: Identify usable supports
paragraphs: Explore skills, relationships, routines, and practical resources with evidence of how they function.

process.title: Choose a realistic application
paragraphs: Connect a resource to an agreed goal and consider barriers, costs, and what additional support is required.

process.title: Review what actually helped
paragraphs: Adapt the plan based on experience. Encouraging language is not enough if the proposed support remains inaccessible.

limits.title: Not forced gratitude
paragraphs: You do not have to find a benefit in loss, injustice, or illness. Care can acknowledge those experiences without trying to balance them away with positive qualities.

limits.title: Not a substitute for specialized treatment
paragraphs: A strengths-based stance can shape care, but it does not establish which treatment is appropriate for a diagnosis or level of risk. The actual clinical plan still needs explanation.

questions.question: What if I cannot name any strengths?
paragraphs: Start with ordinary details rather than a list of admirable traits. What has helped you get through a day? Who knows something important about you? It is also reasonable to say that you first need the difficulty to be understood.

questions.question: Does this mean focusing only on what is going well?
paragraphs: No. A useful approach includes needs, pain, constraints, and risk alongside resources. Ignoring the difficult part would make the picture less accurate, not more strengths-based.

questions.question: Is it a distinct therapy with a fixed program?
paragraphs: The term is broader than one manualized psychotherapy. Ask which clinical methods the therapist uses and how the strengths-based perspective shapes assessment, goals, and practical work.

questions.question: Can a strength also be a problem?
paragraphs: A useful capacity can become costly when overused or unsupported. Being dependable, for example, does not make unlimited responsibility healthy or feasible. Context and choice matter.

questions.question: How would we know the work is useful?
paragraphs: Look for changes connected to your goals: a usable support, a clearer boundary, or an activity that becomes more possible. A positive description of you is not, by itself, a completed treatment outcome.

related.title: Solution-focused therapy
related.text: Explore exceptions and concrete signs of change.

related.title: Person-centered therapy
related.text: Compare an emphasis on empathy and your own perspective.

related.title: Caregiver stress
related.text: Consider responsibilities and support beyond personal effort.
